title: Cold soaking freeze-dried meals: what the manufacturers say
description: Four of five backcountry brands take a position on cold water and one says nothing. Their published times run from 10 minutes to an hour, unreconciled.

sources.title: How to Rehydrate Freeze Dried Food — Tips and Techniques

faq.question: Which backcountry brands say cold soaking is allowed?
faq.answer: Four of five checked take an affirmative position. Mountain House says “if you can't heat water, cold water will also work to rehydrate your Mountain House meal” [2]. ReadyWise says “many of the foods can be re-hydrated and ready to eat with any temperature of water” [10]. Backpacker's Pantry permits it while stating it has not tested it [6][7]. Good To-Go permits it only on its Stove-Free line, which is built for cool water [13]. Peak Refuel publishes no position on any page checked [3][4][5].

faq.question: How long does a cold soak actually take?
faq.answer: The published figures do not agree. Good To-Go's Stove-Free meals state 10 to 12 minutes in cool water [14][15]. ReadyWise gives 5 to 15 minutes and does not attach a time penalty to cold water [11]. Mountain House says roughly twice the hot-water time, which against its own 8-to-9-minute standard works out near 16 to 18 minutes [1][2]. Backpacker's Pantry estimates “upwards of an hour” [6]. That is a six-fold spread and no source reconciles it.

faq.question: Why is Peak Refuel silent about it?
faq.answer: No published reason exists. Eight Peak Refuel pages were checked, including a page titled Hydration that covers the brand's drink mix rather than meal rehydration [5]. Every prep instruction found specifies boiling water: “carefully add 1 1/3 cups (10.5 oz) of boiling water to pouch” [3]. Silence is not permission and it is not refusal; it is an absence, and it should be read as one.

faq.question: Is cold soaking a food-safety problem?
faq.answer: The mechanism is documented and the time limit is not. Utah State Extension states that “freeze-drying does not kill bacteria and/or other microbes. It preserves them” [18], and that “if moisture is reintroduced, such as during rehydration or improper storage, bacteria can become active again” [18][19]. University of Minnesota Extension phrases the same point as microorganisms present before freeze-drying beginning to grow again on rehydration [20]. USDA's danger zone rule, which allows two hours or one hour above 90 °F, is written for perishable prepared food generally [21], and no source found applies it to a dried meal soaking in a pouch.

faq.question: Does it matter whether the meal is freeze-dried or dehydrated?
faq.answer: For safety framing, the extension sources checked do not distinguish the two. They discuss rehydration in general terms [18][19][20]. For prep, the brands do distinguish, and not in one direction. Good To-Go is dehydrated by its own statement, brings its meals to 165 °F in production, and argues freeze-drying “can break down the cell walls of ingredients, resulting in poor texture” [17]; yet it is the brand selling a cool-water line [13]. ReadyWise Outdoor makes the opposite argument, that being freeze-dried is why its meals cold soak: “all the ReadyWise Adventure meals are freeze-dried so regardless of if you have a stove or not you can still cold soak them” [12].

faq.question: Can I cold soak a meal I freeze-dried myself?
faq.answer: No manufacturer or extension source publishes a cold-soak procedure for home-produced meals. Harvest Right's rehydration guidance runs the other way on the two points it does address: hot water for cooked meals, and cold water in the refrigerator only for raw meat, “never room temperature or warm water” [22]. Utah State requires a cooking kill step for foods that would normally be cooked, at 160 °F for beef, 165 °F for poultry and 145 °F for seafood [18]; a cold soak does not perform that step.

bodyHtml:
The short version: four of the five major backcountry brands publish a position on rehydrating with cold water, and their stated times run from 10 minutes to “upwards of an hour”, a six-fold spread that none of them reconciles [6][13][14]. Peak Refuel publishes nothing on the question across every page checked, including one titled Hydration [3][4][5]. Where a brand does publish an instruction, that instruction is the binding one for that meal: follow the directions printed on the pouch you are actually carrying, not a cross-brand summary.

Brand by brand

These are the positions as published, in the brands' own words. “Silent” is a finding in this table, not a blank: it means the pages checked contain no statement either way.

BrandPositionPublished wordingSource
Mountain HousePermitted, framed as a fallback“If you can't heat water, cold water will also work to rehydrate your Mountain House meal.” And: “In a pinch you can use cold water, just give it about twice as long to re-hydrate.”[2][1]
Peak RefuelSilent: no position on any page checkedNone. Prep instructions specify boiling water only: “Carefully add 1 1/3 cups (10.5 oz) of boiling water to pouch.”[3][4][5]
Backpacker's PantryPermitted, explicitly untested“We have not tested rehydrating our meals with cold water. While it should work, it could take upwards of an hour to fully rehydrate the meal.”[6][7]
ReadyWisePermitted, and advocated“Many of the foods can be re-hydrated and ready to eat with any temperature of water.” Its outdoor arm published a piece arguing the case: “You can still cold soak them and have a delicious meal ready when you get to camp.”[10][12]
Good To-GoSplit by product lineStove-Free line: “Prepared with only cool water, in 10 minutes or less!” Standard entrees: “Add a little more than one cup (250ML) of BOILING (yes, boiling) water to bag.”[13][16]

Two details are worth pulling out of that table. First, the silence is narrower than the trail lore suggests; it is one brand, not the category. Peak Refuel's pouches are described as food grade and safe to eat from directly [4], but nothing found addresses water temperature.

Second, Good To-Go's split is internal, and the brand names its own influence. The Stove-Free page credits the practice's origin: “inspired by the ingenuity of thru hikers 'cold-soaking' their backpacking meals to save on pack weight”. It describes traditional cold soaking as carrying hours-long rehydration times and subpar texture, and positions the new line as the answer [13]. The same brand's standard entrees are emphatic in the other direction, with BOILING capitalized on the pouch instructions [16]. Good To-Go is also dehydrated rather than freeze-dried by its own statement [17], so its cool-water figures describe a different process than the freeze-dried brands above it.

Backpacker's Pantry does instruct cold water for one narrow case, which is easy to mistake for a general endorsement: “If you are adding freeze-dried meats to another entree for an added punch of protein, do so in cold water” [8]. That is an instruction about adding an ingredient, not about soaking a meal.

Time cold vs hot

Every figure below is brand-stated. The hot column is what the brand prints for its normal preparation; the cold column is whatever the brand publishes for cold or cool water, which in two cases is nothing.

BrandHot waterCold or cool waterEvidentiary standingSource
Good To-Go, Stove-Free lineNot applicable: cool water only10–12 min (12 min as 6+6; 10 min as 5+5)Productized: a line built and sold for cool water[13][14][15]
ReadyWise5–15 min5–15 min; no stated penalty for coldMarketed capability, no test method published[10][11]
Mountain House8–9 min standard, about 15 min for longer-cooking meals“About twice as long”, no fixed minutes publishedUnqualified; the brand does not say whether it was tested[1][2]
Backpacker's Pantry15 min (8 min, stir, 7 min)“Upwards of an hour”Explicitly untested, brand-stated[6][7][9]
Good To-Go, standard line10–20 min by productNone: boiling onlyInstruction is directive, not silent[16][17]
Peak Refuel10 minNo figure existsSilence[3][4][5]

The four cold figures span 10 minutes to roughly 60. Formulation differences are the obvious candidate explanation: particle size, precooked starches, whether a meal is freeze-dried or a freeze-dried and dehydrated mix. But no brand states that, and inventing the reason would be inventing a finding. The confidence behind the claims also varies more than the claims themselves do: one brand sells a dedicated line, one markets the capability, one permits without qualification, and one says in writing that it never tried it [13][10][2][6].

The food-safety question, from extension and regulators

The mechanism is well documented. The time limit is not documented at all.

Utah State University Extension states it plainly: “Freeze-drying does not kill bacteria and/or other microbes. It preserves them” [18]. The same source describes what rehydration does to that dormant population: “if moisture is reintroduced, such as during rehydration or improper storage, bacteria can become active again” [18][19]. University of Minnesota Extension publishes the same finding in its own words, that on rehydration any illness-causing microorganisms present on the product before freeze-drying may begin growing again [20]. Utah State's remedy is a cooking step: foods rehydrated before eating “should have a 'kill step' that destroys bacteria, such as cooking” [18][19], with 160 °F for beef, 165 °F for poultry and 145 °F for seafood [18].

A cold soak performs no kill step. That is a description of the process, and it is the point at which the published guidance stops.

The nearest regulator figure is USDA's, and it is written about something else. FSIS defines the danger zone as “temperatures between 40 and 140°F when perishable food spoils rapidly” and sets the limit as “not more than one hour in the Danger Zone when temperatures are above 90 °F, and two hours when temperatures are below 90°F” [21]. That rule is stated for perishable and prepared food generally. No source found applies it to a dried meal rehydrating in a pouch, and none of the three extension sources publishes an ambient-rehydration time limit of its own [18][19][20].

QuestionWhat is actually publishedSource
Does freeze-drying kill pathogens?No: “it preserves them”[18]
What does adding water do?Dormant bacteria “can become active again”; microorganisms “may begin growing again”[18][19][20]
What removes them?A cooking kill step; 160 °F beef, 165 °F poultry, 145 °F seafood[18]
Is there a time limit for ambient rehydration?None published by any extension service or regulator located[18][19][20]
What is the closest regulator rule?USDA danger zone: 40–140 °F; 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90 °F, written for perishable food generally[21]
Do the sources distinguish freeze-dried from dehydrated here?No: all three discuss rehydration safety in general terms[18][19][20]

Two practical consequences follow from what is published, without extending it. A meal whose ingredients would normally require cooking is not made otherwise by soaking, and Harvest Right's own rehydration guidance handles that case by temperature and location rather than by time: raw meat rehydrates in cold water in the refrigerator, “never room temperature or warm water” [22]. And a soak is an ambient-temperature operation by definition, so what the published safety literature actually turns on is the meal's own composition: precooked or not, meat-bearing or not.

How much popular advice has no source

Cold soaking is heavily discussed and lightly documented. Set against what the brands, extension services and regulators publish, a large share of the common guidance traces to no source in those tiers at all.

Commonly repeatedStatus in published sources
“Soak it for X minutes and it's safe”No source publishes a safe cold-soak duration. Extension gives the reactivation mechanism with no time limit [18][19][20]; USDA's hour and two-hour figures are for perishable prepared food and are not applied to dried meals [21]
“Freeze-dried cold soaks faster than dehydrated”Asserted by one brand about its own products [12] and contradicted in effect by another brand's dehydrated line hitting 10 minutes [13][15]. No comparative source found
“It's roughly double the hot time”That is Mountain House's figure for Mountain House meals [1]. It does not match ReadyWise's no-penalty claim [11] or Backpacker's Pantry's hour [6]
“Every brand works cold, they just won't say so”Four of five do say so, in writing [2][6][10][13]. The one silence is Peak Refuel [3][4][5], and silence is not a concealed yes
“Cold soaking is fine because the food was already cooked”No brand or extension source found states this as a safety rationale. Good To-Go publishes a 165 °F production temperature for its dehydrated meals [17]; nothing extends that to a rehydration safety claim
Rehydration ratio charts attributed to freeze-dryer manufacturersHarvest Right publishes a method, not a chart: water needed is “roughly equal to the amount of moisture removed,” determined by weighing before and after [22]

If you are cold soaking a meal you freeze-dried and packed yourself, none of the brand figures above apply to it. They describe specific commercial formulations, and no source publishes a cold-soak procedure for home-produced meals.

What we could not source

  • A cold-soak or ambient-rehydration time limit for dried food. Extension establishes that rehydration reactivates dormant microbes [18][19][20] but publishes no time limit analogous to USDA's one-hour and two-hour rule [21].
  • Any application of the USDA danger-zone rule to dried-meal rehydration. The rule is stated for perishable and prepared food generally [21]; no source connects it to a soaking pouch.
  • Any source distinguishing freeze-dried from dehydrated for rehydration safety. All three extension sources treat rehydration in general terms [18][19][20].
  • A stated reason for the six-fold spread in cold-soak times. Formulation differences are plausible; no brand publishes them as the explanation [6][10][13].
  • Any Peak Refuel statement on water temperature. Eight pages were checked, including product pages, the FAQ and a page titled Hydration that covers the brand's drink mix rather than meal rehydration [3][4][5].
  • Test methodology behind any brand's cold-water claim. Backpacker's Pantry is the only brand that discloses its standing, by stating it has not tested [6][7]. The others state a position without one.
  • A cold-soak procedure for home freeze-dried meals. Harvest Right publishes hot-water guidance for cooked meals and a refrigerator-only cold rule for raw meat [22]; nothing found addresses cold soaking on the trail.
